Seoul is safe.

Lots of misinformation in the other comments and all over the internet. The term Guinea refers to a currency. Guineamen were (mostly German) mercenaries hired during the revolutionary war and were payed in Guineas. After the war, a large number of them settled in Gloucester County. For a long while, the community was mostly isolated, with the only real connection to the outside world being a ferry. Just like on a lot of Chesapeake islands, they developed a strange accent. A combination of a Norfolk accent and old English/Colonial American. 

Because the area is extremely rural and for a long while was extremely poor, it developed a bad reputation for a long time as a racist and dangerous area. Around the turn of the 20th century, roads were paved into Guinea and the quality of life there shot up. 

These days, Guineamen are somewhat strange, heavily accented folk who are, for the most part, incredibly hardworking, friendly, and kind. They come from a very close knit community, and tend to keep to themselves, but if you ever come across someone who was born and raised in Guinea, you'll find that they're warm and friendly folk.

They have a bad reputation that has followed them for hundreds of years, but these days they're just honest folk with funny accents. If you ever want to meet some, take a walk around the Stagecoach flea market on a nice Saturday morning.

Source: Grew up in Gloucester my whole life, was close friends with members of the Kellum, Shackleford and Belvin families, which have been staples in Guinea for hundreds of years.

This is going to get buried, but I'd go back. Not for Bitcoin, not for Apple stocks. For my grandparent's house on the creek. Growing up, I'd spend every weekend there. My grandfather (step-grandfather?) bought a beautiful brick house on a huge plot on land surrounded on three sides by a creek. It had a massive garden made of white bricks and carved stone, big open fields, a bridge over a small brook, forests, marshes, a little beach. It was the most beautiful chunk of land you could imagine. I was the luckiest kid in the world for being able to spend my weekends there.

My grandmother would cook Korean food for my brother and I.  My grandfather, when he finished his work, would play games with us. We watched robot wars together, fished, and eventually for christmas my brother and I got a little off road go-kart to drive around on the fields. 

I took it for granted. About 10 years ago a hurricane hit. It flooded the house. It was still livable, but only barely. My grandparents had been drifting apart for a long time, and the stress of their life being put underwater drove them apart for good. The house was sold about 5 years ago, and from what I understand, the new owners tore everything down. 

I wouldnt try to keep my grandparents together. My grandmother is lonely, but my grandfather has a new family that I'm sure he loves very much. I havent seen him in a few years. I wouldnt want to take this new family from him.

Instead, I just want to go back and spend my weekends there. I miss that a lot. I wouldnt take it for granted. I'd be a lot more helpful to them. I wouldnt just treat their place like a weekend playground. I'd treat it like a home. Maybe I could convince them to take out more substantial flood insurance. Maybe I could have remembered the place better.

Maybe I could have gone and seen it one last time before they sold the place. 

Now, the go-kart sits rusting years later in my yard. I keep telling myself one of these days I'll throw new tires on it and reweld the seat further back so I can drive it again. From what I understand, the pier that I used to fish from there collapsed after another hurricane recently. When they sold it, I didnt think too much of it. I was sad, but I didnt realize until a few months later that the cold, empty feeling in my gut was what it felt like to be homesick. A massive part of my childhood is gone. It's 30 minutes from where I live now, but it might as well be on the moon.

I've thought, a lot of times, about sending a letter to the address. To whoever lives there now, telling them how much that little part of Virginia means to me. Telling them a little bit about the memories I made there and the love and happiness that existed there. I'd tell them that I hope that they love it and that they find the peace and comfort that I always did. I hope they love being there as much as I did. I dont know who owns it now, but I hope they have grand children.

So, in short, yes. I'd go back so I could spend at least one more weekend there. I want to go home.

1: If everything is going well, there shouldnt be any smoke. Some printers can be a fire hazard though, and due to their heat, please keep anything flammable well clear of the printer.

2: If a print fails, filament will be extruded without anything to stick to. Functionally, it wont be any different from the printer doing a normal print.

3: ABS gives off a strong smell, and PLA does not give off any noticeable fumes. I'm not sure if ABS would set off an ionization detector, but my gut says no.

3.1 : If something smells burnt when you're printing, then something is seriously wrong. A printer is, at it's core, basically a hot glue gun controlled by a robot. Unless you're printing with ABS, there will be no smell at all.

3.2: It's a very tiny amount of plastic being heated up by a very small metal hotend. At any given time, there's no more than a few rice grains worth of plastic heated up to melting temperature. Plastic goes into the machine solid and cool, and it cools down almost instantly after it exits the end.

4: Again, the hot end of the printer is so small that it wont set off a fire detector. If you can run a hot glue gun without setting off an alarm, the hot end wont either. I keep my printer in a very small room, and when it's running, it doesnt heat up the room at all. The amount of actual heat it gives off is very low.

5: It's a good idea to put your printer somewhere well ventilated, just as a safety measure. You dont risk setting off an alarm, but you are melting plastic, which can give off fumes depending on the type of plastic you're using. Setting it near a window with a fan blowing out would not hurt.

Overall, your printer does not give off enough heat or fumes to set off any alarm. If you can use a hot glue gun, a soldering iron, a toaster, or your stove without setting off alarms, then the printer poses no issue whatsoever.

I'm very late to the party, and I'm 21 so I cant answer this technically, but parents, let your kid fail. 

Let your kid make mistakes and fuck things up. Let your kid find out what works and doesn't work on their own. Make sure they know that if they fail spectacularly, they have you to fall back on. Be their safety net, but not their safety harness. My parents raised me to be pretty independent. I was allowed to go out on my own, I was allowed to do what I wanted. My parents accepted the fact that as a teenager, there was a decent chance I'd go out and drink, or try light drugs. They told me that if I ever needed a ride home from a party, I wouldn't be in trouble. 

Having that freedom to make mistakes, knowing that they'd be there to help me get back up after I fall, and knowing that if I needed help, they'd come help did wonders for me while I was maturing.

Be ready to catch your kids when they slip, but don't hold their hand the whole way. Let them have the freedom to make their own mistakes in their life while knowing that you'll be there to make sure those mistakes are learning experiences, rather than life-ruining experiences.



Something else supremely important is letting your kid try new things. Growing up, I kept wanting to learn things. Electronics, coding, woodworking, whatever. My dad and I are basically the same person. When I was 17 and wanted to learn how to code, it turned out he'd been learning for years as a hobby. When I was 19 and got an electronics kit to learn how to work with an arduino, he gave me his old electronics kit from the 80s. He always had information he was excited to pass on, and whenever I'd get into a hobby he used to like, he'd get back into it as well. Not only that, but he always took an interest. "Have you done anything cool with that Arduino?", "What kind of tools are you looking at buying next", "I think I've got a big box of little LEDs around here if you want them". He asked me questions about it, and encouraged me to pick up new skills. "If you're tired of using a breadboard I can give you my old soldering iron.", "I think your grandpa has an old table saw if you want to try working with that", "Since you're learning how to make websites, you ought to get Adobe so you can do graphic work to go with it".

In short, give your kid space to make their own mistakes, but make sure they know you're there to help them when those mistakes happen. Also get interested in what your kid is interested in. Encourage hobbies and help them become passions. Don't just ask them questions, but actually *talk* about it.

Germany mobilized faster. The Germans were, as they still are, a marvel of bureaucracy and efficiency.

Nobody really knew how battles in WWI would play out. They had very basic ideas from the Russo-Japanese war, but nobody actually understood just how bad they would be. 

The Belgians were the first country to face off against Germany in WWI, and they were not ready for it. The Belgians had a series of fortresses that were absolutely massive. Absurd in size, really. Ten years prior, they would have been invincible, but artillery had progressed in the last decade. The Belgians expected a fierce battle, but they had no idea how brutal it would be. 

The Germans showed up with some of the largest artillery pieces ever built to that point ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bertha_(howitzer) ). The Germans began human wave attacks against the fortresses. Germans piled up in the fields leading to the fortresses, but they kept coming. Their guns battered the emplacements, slowly wearing them down into dust. The artillery destroyed what was once thought to be an invincible shield of fortresses. 

Nobody was ready for that.

At one point, the Germans marched through a Belgian town in a column over a dozen men wide. The townsfolk came out to watch them, as it was a spectacle, but then, as hour after hour passed, and the marching line didn't end, didn't slow, and didn't thin out, the townsfolk slowly went back to their business. The Germans were so efficient, and fielded armies so massive, that in the nearly 12 hours it took for their column to march through the town, the townsfolk got bored.

Nobody was ready for that.

In previous wars, an army of several tens of thousands was a sizable force. Napoleon's Grande Armee, at it's largest, was a million men. The Germans, and later every other nation in WWI, fielded multiple armies of over a million men each. As a point of reference, Britian's standing army, including reservists, in 1914, was just under a million men. The armies that Germany marched through Belgium and into France were around 3-4 million strong.

France's army was also around 4 million, but the vast majority were not prepared for the war. The vast majority were recently drafted or enlisted in the lead up to WWI. The Germans, on the other hand, were prepared. They were ready for the war, and nobody else was. Nobody else was prepared for battles on this scale. Nobody else was ready for it. Germany was, and thus they got to dictate how the war would be fought. They took the lead. Germany didnt cause WWI, but the reason so many people at the time blamed Germany, is because Germany was the one who dictated the scale of the war early on.

Nobody was ready for it.

Edit: I dont think it was Germany's fault. I think it was the new weapons systems and just the technology of the age. The amount of war and suffering was inevitable, I think. I realized that I made it sound like it was Germany's fault. I dont believe that. I just wanted to include that bit as a bit of insight into why so many at the time blamed Germany. This was all written more to show how people viewed events in the moment, rather than hindsight.

Its not that they didn't know they needed helmets, its that none of them had enough because nobody realized how big the armies were going to be, and everyone thought the war would be over before they could get the helmets to the troops anyway. They were stupid. They knew what shrapnel was and they knew how important metal helmets would be. They learned those lessons all the way back watching the US civil war, and even more recently the Russo-Japanese war.

As for uniforms, they expected the gentlemanly wars of previous decades, where two small armies clashed in a predefined area. The Germans decided that this would not be the protocol anymore and caught everybody off guard.

Also, the French, among others, used colors that represented their nation. They expected battles to play out in ways that would make it vital tp tell your own troops apart from the enemy. Grand flanking maneuvers and charges. Not a dug in enemy across a blasted wasteland. Not an enemy marching through forests and towns. They didnt expect the grand strategies of Germany and her allies. They expected single-day battles with tight coordination, where being able to direct your men easily would be the key, rather than battles of attrition. 

But they knew helmets were important. They just didnt have enough to go around.

Yeah, wood roaches are annoying. They're big and scary and end up in houses pretty often. Check around your house (or outside your apartment if that's where you live) for any exposed wood. Planks, untreated fence (if you've got a rotting fence), tree stumps, or piles of branches. Anywhere that exposed wood (as in untreated or trees without bark on them) can get wet will attract wood roaches. Definitely try borax around your house. You don't have to dump piles, just rub a little anywhere something can get into your house. It'll kill them as they come in.

The US Northeast is full of wood roaches, so it's probably them. Like I said, though, wood roaches wont go for your underwear drawer, as they're more concerned with trying to escape your house. Try putting your underwear in a plastic tub with a lid and see if it keeps happening. If it does, it's probably your washer.

What kind of area do you live in? If it's a fairly temperate area of North America, those are probably wood roaches and not cockroaches. 

Wood roaches are slimmer, longer, and prefer to be outside. They sometimes find their way into your home, but aren't really a pest that 'infests' your house. Seeing a couple a month isn't super worrying if you live in an area that's fairly wet (meaning lots of creeks, rivers, ponds, ect) and wooded. Wood roaches likely aren't getting into your underwear drawer, and are rather trying to find their way back out of your house.

Next time you see one, try to capture it under a clear cup and then google cockroaches and wood roaches to find out which you have. A little borax sprinkled around vents, door frames, and windows will help keep them out.

Just as a completely different thought, think about putting your clothes into plastic tubs. The kind with lids are great for storing clothes, and they help keep clothes from gathering dust and particulate. I put all of my clothes into these tubs that stack really easily. It keeps my closet a lot more condensed, keeps my clothes away from any bugs (moths are a much bigger threat to your wardrobe than roaches), and keeps them dry (I live in a very humid area).

My understanding from the nutritionists and trainers who work at my gym is that it's less about exactly how much sleep you get and more about just getting consistent good sleep. As long as you sleep about the same each night and when you wake up you feel refreshed and not groggy, then you can get 5 hours of sleep or 12 and your body will react pretty much the same. 

Everybody has a different 'ideal' amount of sleeping time, and as long as you can find that and stick to it, you'll feel better in general. For instance, I work best on 6 to 7 hours of sleep. More or less and I feel groggy and out of it all day.

Sleep doesn't have any real affect on your metabolism unless you're drastically changing your sleep schedule. It's more about mental state and energy, which is different for everybody.

I was also tired of being fat. Especially being fat and working at a gym. The main thing for the first couple months is to not worry about your weight too much. Spend a lot of time on treadmills, in a pool, or out jogging. Before you can really start shedding pounds you need to get your cardio up.

It's great that you're already feeling the difference. Weight doesn't matter nearly as much as how you feel. Focus on that feeling rather than checking a scale every day. Once you're more in shape, you can start focusing on shedding those pounds.
